foundation.description: Start from zero. We'll skip the academic jargon and jump straight into how Python actually tracks state, makes decisions, and runs your logic. You'll see memory behave live.

beginner.description: Time to build real engineering habits. We'll trace how loops, functions, and arrays actually work under the hood so you don't just guess-and-run your scripts.

intermediate.description: Upgrade your toolkit. We'll dive into dictionaries, stacks, queues, and classic searches. These are the daily drivers you'll use in every backend you ever build.

advanced.description: Start thinking algorithmically. Watch how recursion builds up call stacks, see sorting in real-time, and finally actually understand why Big O notation matters in prod.

mastery.description: The deep end. This is where we stop writing scripts and start engineering systems. Master the graph algorithms and dynamic programming patterns that get you through staff-level screens.

algorithms.hello-world: Your real entry point. See exactly how print() dumps data to standard out—because trust me, print debugging never really goes away.
algorithms.variables-types: Watch variables claim memory. Understand ints vs floats vs strings, and see why dynamically typed languages like Python let you get away with murder.
algorithms.string-operations: Strings are just fancy arrays. See slicing, slicing with steps, and concatenation. In a web backend, string manipulation is 80% of what you'll do.
algorithms.arithmetic: Math under the hood. See precisely how Python evaluates complex expressions, and learn about the quirks of float division versus integer division.
algorithms.if-else: The core of business logic. Watch branching happen in real-time and see why getting your truthiness operators wrong is the source of endless auth bugs.
algorithms.while-loop: Repetition until a condition trips. See the guard check fire before every iteration and learn how to avoid accidentally DDoS-ing your own machine.
algorithms.for-loop: The workhorse of data processing. See how Python iterators yank elements from collections one by one—this is what powers massive data pipelines.
algorithms.lists-basics: Python's god-tier container. Watch memory shift as we append, pop, and index into arrays. Understand why inserting in the middle is secretly expensive.
algorithms.functions-intro: The building block of clean code. See how calling a function pauses execution, allocates a new stack frame, and pipes the return value back.
algorithms.input-output: Programs that talk back. See how fetching input blocks the main thread completely until the user responds—and why type casting is mandatory.
algorithms.linear-search: Brute-force check every element. O(n) is the simplest search there is—and frankly, for small arrays in memory, it's usually all you need.
algorithms.count-occurrences: Building a frequency map. Watch a hash dictionary accumulate tallies in a single pass. This is a foundational pattern for log analysis.
algorithms.find-min-max: Tracking boundaries. Look at how one pass is enough to track both limits simultaneously without wasting CPU cycles sorting the data.
algorithms.sum-average: The accumulator pattern. See how sum() elegantly iterates arrays underneath. You'll write this pattern a thousand times before you retire.
algorithms.loop-explorer: Watch how loop bodies modify shared state variables across passes. Getting iteration boundaries right is how you prevent off-by-one errors in prod.
algorithms.reverse-list: The two-pointer squeeze. Watch them march inward and swap elements. A classic O(n) in-place technique that saves you from allocating new arrays.
algorithms.palindrome: Symmetry checking. See how the two-pointer approach confirms matches from both ends while instantly bailing at the first failed check.
algorithms.fizzbuzz: The classic interview gatekeeper. See how modulo operators dictate flow control across a loop, and why the order of your conditions is everything.
algorithms.factorial: Multiplying 1 to n. Witness the accumulator pattern grow exponentially. This teaches you why base conditions and correctly starting at 1 (not 0) are vital.
algorithms.fibonacci-iterative: Generating sequences with rolling variables. Understand why tracking just the last two values in O(1) space completely destroys the recursive approach.
algorithms.binary-search: The foundation of database indices. Watch how aggressively O(log n) searches eliminate half the problem at every step, requiring sorted inputs first.
algorithms.selection-sort: Scan for the absolute minimum, then anchor it at the front. It guarantees exactly n-1 swaps—useful in systems where writing data is much costlier than reading it.
algorithms.insertion-sort: Slide elements left until they hit order. It's actually incredibly fast for naturally 'nearly sorted' data, which happens in the real world constantly.
algorithms.two-pointers: Converging indices. See how marching a left and right pointer can elegantly solve array problems in O(n) time, bypassing the classic O(n²) double loop.
algorithms.hash-map-counting: The O(1) dictionary trick. This is the bedrock for counting frequencies—an essential pattern when you're querying fast instead of looping slow.
algorithms.stack-ops: Last In, First Out (LIFO). Push, pop, and peek your way to understanding how undo-trees, browser histories, and function call stacks actually operate.
algorithms.queue-ops: First In, First Out (FIFO). Tasks in, tasks out. This animates the core mechanism behind task workers, event loops, and rate limiters.
algorithms.anagram-check: Are these strings just scrambled? Watch how mapping character frequencies in a dictionary solves this gracefully without the overhead of sorting strings.
algorithms.sliding-window: Gliding a fixed frame over an array. See how it subtracts the outgoing element and adds the incoming one, saving you from disastrous O(n*k) recalculations.
algorithms.merge-sorted: Zipper two sorted arrays together. This is the cornerstone sub-routine that powers the beast that is Merge Sort.
algorithms.bubble-sort: The classic teaching tool. You'll never ship this slow O(n²) sort to production, but watching adjacent elements swap teaches invaluable loop boundary mechanics.
algorithms.merge-sort: Divide, branch, and conquer. Watch the recursion split arrays down to single elements, then seamlessly stitch them back into sorted perfection. A fast, stable O(n log n) engine.
algorithms.quick-sort: The workhorse sort. Pick a pivot, partition around it, and recurse. It's fast, boasts legendary cache locality, but see why bad pivots cause worst-case nightmares.
algorithms.heap-sort: Visualize the max-heap. Pull the highest priority element out and re-balance. It guarantees O(n log n) even in worst-cases, heavily utilized in priority-queue systems.
algorithms.bfs: Explore outward like a ripple. See Breadth-First Search utilize a queue to guarantee the shortest path in unweighted networks—essential for pathfinding.
algorithms.dfs: Plunge deep before backtracking. Depth-First Search stacks recursive calls, perfect for exhausting possibilities in maze solving or topological sorting.
algorithms.binary-tree-traversal: Navigating the node network. See the dramatic differences when you process roots before, between, or after children (pre/in/post-order).
algorithms.two-sum: The most famous leetcode question. See how building an on-the-fly hash map trades a tiny bit of RAM to nosedive the time complexity down to O(n).
algorithms.valid-parentheses: The ultimate stack test. Watch pushing openers and popping them when a closer arrives—this is literally how your code compiler checks syntax.
algorithms.fibonacci-recursive: Exponential explosion. Watch the call tree branch out horrifyingly out of control. An excellent warning on why raw recursion desperately needs memoization.
algorithms.dijkstra: The backbone of Google Maps. Watch Dijkstra's leverage a priority queue to definitively find cheapest routes across weighted graphs, completely dodging cycles.
algorithms.knapsack: The DP classic. You have a weight limit; cram in the max value. See the 2D matrix build up sub-answers row by row so you don't repeat work.
algorithms.lcs: Longest Common Subsequence. Core to how `git diff` works. Watch DP align two strings character by character without scrambling their relative order.
algorithms.topological-sort: Task resolution. See Kahn’s algorithm strip out zero-dependency nodes one by one—the exact logic underlying package managers like npm or pip.
algorithms.kruskals: Spanning trees on a budget. Greedily grab the cheapest edges and rely on a union-find structure to guarantee you never accidentally close a cycle.
algorithms.trie: The auto-complete engine. Watch strings break into single-character nodes, building a prefix tree that makes searching incredibly scalable over massive dictionaries.
algorithms.floyd-warshall: All pairs, everywhere. A savage 3-nested-loop DP that updates a massive matrix until it knows the shortest path between literally every single node.
algorithms.segment-tree: Fast interval crunching. Watch the tree build upwards, enabling O(log n) range queries and point updates. Perfect for high-frequency live dashboard stats.
algorithms.coin-change: Finding exact change with minimal coins. See how dynamic programming sweeps away the failures of the greedy approach when coin denominations get weird.
algorithms.bit-manipulation: Bare metal mechanics. AND, OR, XOR, and bit-shifts. These power cryptography, graphics systems, and crazy low-level micro-optimizations. Learn to speak CPU.

hello-world.title: Knowledge Check
hello-world.question: What does the `print()` function do?
hello-world.successMessage: Spot on! `print()` is your lifeline for dumping state to the console. Even seniors use it daily for quick sanity checks.

variables-types.title: Knowledge Check
variables-types.question: Which of the following creates an integer variable?
variables-types.successMessage: Correct. In Python, an int is an int. Drop quotes, drop decimals. Clean and simple memory allocation.

string-operations.title: Knowledge Check
string-operations.question: Which operator connects two strings in Python?
string-operations.successMessage: Nailed it. The `+` operator overloads specifically to stitch strings together. Just watch out for adding ints to strings—that'll crash the script.

arithmetic.title: Knowledge Check
arithmetic.question: What does the modulo operator (%) return?
arithmetic.successMessage: Exactly. Modulo `%` is the remainder. We use this constantly to check if things are even, odd, or cycling over array boundaries.

if-else.title: Knowledge Check
if-else.question: Which keyword is used for alternative conditions in Python?
if-else.successMessage: Correct. `elif` saves us from deeply nesting `else if` statements. Keep your cyclomatic complexity flat and your code stays readable.

while-loop.title: Knowledge Check
while-loop.question: What happens if a while loop's condition never becomes False?
while-loop.successMessage: Right! A guard condition that never goes `False` blocks the main thread completely. Kiss your CPU goodbye.

for-loop.title: Knowledge Check
for-loop.question: Which built-in function is typically used with for loops to iterate numbers?
for-loop.successMessage: Yep, `range()` is the standard factory for pushing out integer sequences. Perfect for indexing or running a block exactly N times.

lists-basics.title: Knowledge Check
lists-basics.question: How do you access the first element of list 'arr'?
lists-basics.successMessage: Correct. Arrays are 0-indexed across almost every language, because the index represents the memory offset from the start of the array.

functions-intro.title: Knowledge Check
functions-intro.question: What keyword defines a function?
functions-intro.successMessage: Exactly. `def` allocates that block as a callable object. Reusability is everything; don't repeat yourself inside scripts.

input-output.title: Knowledge Check
input-output.question: What type does input() always return?
input-output.successMessage: Correct! `input()` always dumps a string payload. Remember: you MUST cast it via `int()` or `float()` to do math on it.

linear-search.title: Knowledge Check
linear-search.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search?
linear-search.successMessage: Correct. It's O(n) brute force. Sure it scales linearly, but frankly, if the dataset is small, it's totally acceptable in prod.

count-occurrences.title: Knowledge Check
count-occurrences.question: What does 'count occurrences' do?

options.A: Counts how many times a value appears in the list

count-occurrences.successMessage: Spot on. Tallying via hash map is an essential aggregation pattern when doing raw data processing or log analysis.

find-min-max.title: Knowledge Check
find-min-max.question: How many passes over the list are needed to find both the minimum and maximum?
find-min-max.successMessage: Absolutely. One loop is enough when you stash both the running highest and lowest states. Avoid sorting just to find extremums.

sum-average.title: Knowledge Check
sum-average.question: Which Python built-in returns the sum of all elements in a list?
sum-average.successMessage: Correct. `sum()` is extremely hyper-optimized in C underneath. Trust the built-in standard library over rolling your own loop here.

loop-explorer.title: Knowledge Check
loop-explorer.question: Which Python keyword exits a loop immediately?
loop-explorer.successMessage: Right! `break` decisively kills the loop mid-execution. Use it to short-circuit processing the moment you find what you need.

reverse-list.title: Knowledge Check
reverse-list.question: What does arr[::-1] return in Python?

options.D: A copy of the list unchanged

reverse-list.successMessage: Exactly. Slicing with `[::-1]` allocates a new, flipped copy. It's elegant Pythonic sugar, though technically not O(1) in-place space.

palindrome.title: Knowledge Check
palindrome.question: A palindrome reads the same...
palindrome.successMessage: Correct. Testing symmetry from both ends simultaneously is the classic two-pointer validation pattern.

fizzbuzz.title: Knowledge Check
fizzbuzz.question: In FizzBuzz, what is printed for a number divisible by both 3 and 5?
fizzbuzz.successMessage: Nailed it. Overlapping conditions (like modulo 15) must be checked *first*, or the single conditions will incorrectly trap the execution.

factorial.title: Knowledge Check
factorial.question: What is the value of 0! (zero factorial)?
factorial.successMessage: Yup, the empty product is mathematically 1. Essential when your accumulator loops need a clean, non-zero multiplicative start.

fibonacci-iterative.title: Knowledge Check
fibonacci-iterative.question: In the Fibonacci sequence, each number equals...

options.B: The sum of the two preceding numbers

fibonacci-iterative.successMessage: Correct! Tracking just the last two values avoids eating immense amounts of memory. Good algorithms minimize state.

binary-search.title: Knowledge Check
binary-search.question: What must be true about an array before applying Binary Search?

options.A: It must have an even length

binary-search.successMessage: Correct! Slashing the search space by half yields breathtaking performance on huge arrays, but don't forget it mandates pre-sorted data.

selection-sort.title: Knowledge Check
selection-sort.question: In Selection Sort, what happens during each pass?

options.A: The largest element bubbles to the end
options.B: The array is divided in half
options.C: The minimum element is found and swapped to the front

selection-sort.successMessage: Exactly. Unlike other basic sorts, it locks down exactly one swap per pass. Good for environments where writing to disk/memory is highly throttled.

insertion-sort.title: Knowledge Check
insertion-sort.question: Insertion Sort is most efficient when applied to...
insertion-sort.successMessage: Right. It performs bizarrely well on lists that are 'almost sorted'—which is why elite sort algorithms (like Timsort) fall back to it.

two-pointers.title: Knowledge Check
two-pointers.question: In a sorted array two-pointer sum problem, if the current sum is too large, what should you do?
two-pointers.successMessage: Correct! Pinching the bounds inward lets you gracefully skip entire ranges of bad combinations, plunging O(n²) time down to O(n).

hash-map-counting.title: Knowledge Check
hash-map-counting.question: What is the average-case time complexity for a hash map lookup?
hash-map-counting.successMessage: Nailed it. Hashmaps give you O(1) amortized reads. Stashing state like this is how you cheat your way out of doing nested loops.

stack-ops.title: Knowledge Check
stack-ops.question: In a Stack, which element is removed first (LIFO principle)?
stack-ops.successMessage: Correct. The Last In is the First Out. Any time you find yourself needing to 'undo' or 'rewind' operations, you need a stack.

queue-ops.title: Knowledge Check
queue-ops.question: In a Queue, which element is served first (FIFO principle)?
queue-ops.successMessage: Right. First In, First Out. This underpins message brokers, task runners, and basically all async queueing architectures.

anagram-check.title: Knowledge Check
anagram-check.question: Two strings are anagrams of each other if they contain...

options.A: The same characters in the same order
options.B: The same characters in any order
options.D: Characters that start the same way

anagram-check.successMessage: Correct! Don't sort the strings (which takes O(n log n)). Just hash the character counts in O(n) and compare dictionaries.

sliding-window.title: Knowledge Check
sliding-window.question: The sliding window technique typically reduces time complexity from...
sliding-window.successMessage: Exactly. Don't recalculate the entire window! Add the right edge, instantly subtract the left edge. O(1) transitions.

merge-sorted.title: Knowledge Check
merge-sorted.question: Merging two sorted arrays of sizes m and n takes time...
merge-sorted.successMessage: Spot on. Zipping them together is incredibly fast (O(m+n)) and serves as the workhorse logic for Merge Sort.

bubble-sort.title: Knowledge Check
bubble-sort.question: After one complete pass of Bubble Sort over an unsorted array, what is guaranteed?

options.B: The largest unsorted element is at its final position
options.C: The array is split in half

bubble-sort.successMessage: Correct. The heaviest elements 'bubble' rightward. And again—never, ever ship this to production if performance matters.

merge-sort.title: Knowledge Check
merge-sort.question: What is the time complexity of Merge Sort in all cases?
merge-sort.successMessage: Correct! It splits log n times and merges over n elements, delivering that rock-solid O(n log n) bound we love.

quick-sort.title: Knowledge Check
quick-sort.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort?
quick-sort.successMessage: Yep, bad pivots trigger devastating O(n²) performance drops. Modern implementations randomize pivots specifically to avoid this trap.

heap-sort.title: Knowledge Check
heap-sort.question: What data structure does Heap Sort rely on?
heap-sort.successMessage: Correct! Max-heaps guarantee you're plucking the highest remaining value out in log n time, keeping the sort completely sorted.

counting-sort.title: Knowledge Check
counting-sort.question: What type of input does Counting Sort work best with?

options.B: Integers within a small, known range

counting-sort.successMessage: Right. When you have tiny, bound integer ranges, you completely bypass the slow O(n log n) comparisons of typical sorts.

recursion-basics.title: Knowledge Check
recursion-basics.question: What prevents a recursive function from running forever?
recursion-basics.successMessage: Correct. A missing base case translates to a blown call stack. Always anchor your recursive loops.

dp-basics.title: Knowledge Check
dp-basics.question: What technique does Dynamic Programming use to avoid recomputing subproblems?
dp-basics.successMessage: Absolutely. Caching previous permutations stops exponential slowdown. DP is just 'remembering the past so you don't repeat it'.

bfs.title: Knowledge Check
bfs.question: Which data structure does Breadth-First Search use to explore nodes level by level?
bfs.successMessage: Yes! A Queue mechanically ensures you scrape all adjacent neighbors first before diving deeper.

dfs.title: Knowledge Check
dfs.question: Which data structure does Depth-First Search naturally use (recursively)?
dfs.successMessage: Right. The Call Stack fundamentally acts as an implicit stack data structure, propelling you deep into a path before backtracking out.

binary-tree-traversal.title: Knowledge Check
binary-tree-traversal.question: Which traversal order visits nodes as Left → Root → Right?
binary-tree-traversal.successMessage: Correct. In-order tree traversal against a Binary Search Tree natively streams the values out completely sorted.

two-sum.title: Knowledge Check
two-sum.question: What data structure makes Two Sum solvable in O(n) time?
two-sum.successMessage: Spot on. It caches the complements in a hash map. It's the ultimate example of trading a little RAM for a massive speedup.

valid-parentheses.title: Knowledge Check
valid-parentheses.question: Which data structure is used to solve Valid Parentheses?
valid-parentheses.successMessage: Correct. Pushing openers and immediately matching them to incoming closers is how compilers actively parse your code syntax.

fibonacci-recursive.title: Knowledge Check
fibonacci-recursive.question: What is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci (no memoization)?
fibonacci-recursive.successMessage: Right. Without caching, the function insanely computes the exact same nodes endlessly. Exponential O(2ⁿ) time will freeze your box instantly.

dijkstra.title: Knowledge Check
dijkstra.question: What is required for Dijkstra's algorithm to produce correct results?

options.B: The graph must be a tree
options.C: All edge weights must be non-negative

dijkstra.successMessage: Correct! Dijkstra is blissfully unaware of negative weights—it'd plunge into infinite cycles. Keep weights strictly non-negative.

bellman-ford.title: Knowledge Check
bellman-ford.question: What advantage does Bellman-Ford have over Dijkstra's algorithm?

options.A: It is faster on dense graphs
options.C: It correctly handles negative edge weights

bellman-ford.successMessage: Yep! It'll tolerate negative weights by relentlessly relaxing edges V-1 times. Fantastic algorithm, though mathematically heavier.

knapsack.title: Knowledge Check
knapsack.question: The 0/1 Knapsack problem is solved using which technique?
knapsack.successMessage: Spot on. A DP matrix caches sub-answers so you can figure out exact maximal loading without rerunning the combinations.

lcs.title: Knowledge Check
lcs.question: What does LCS stand for?
lcs.successMessage: Correct! Tracking characters that persist in the same relative order is the exact logic `git diff` uses to highlight code changes.

topological-sort.title: Knowledge Check
topological-sort.question: Topological Sort is only applicable to which type of graph?
topological-sort.successMessage: Exactly. It's impossible to linearly sequence tasks if they circularly depend on each other. DAGs only.

kruskals.title: Knowledge Check
kruskals.question: Kruskal's algorithm is used to find the...
kruskals.successMessage: Right on! Always grab the cheapest edge possible and instantly rely on union-find checks to prevent horrific cycle loops.

trie.title: Knowledge Check
trie.question: A Trie data structure is most commonly used for...
trie.successMessage: Correct! Prefix routing turns staggering datasets into ultra-fast, shallow traversals—which is inherently what makes 'autocomplete' pop up so fast.

floyd-warshall.title: Knowledge Check
floyd-warshall.question: Floyd-Warshall computes...
floyd-warshall.successMessage: Yep. It crushes through absolutely every permutation of midpoints until the shortest distances across V nodes are fully locked.

segment-tree.title: Knowledge Check
segment-tree.question: A Segment Tree supports range queries in what time complexity?
segment-tree.successMessage: Correct! A structural tree dramatically shrinks painful linear sweeping. This allows you to surgically pull out and update ranges instantly.

coin-change.title: Knowledge Check
coin-change.question: Coin Change (minimum coins) is best solved using...
coin-change.successMessage: Right. Standard greedy loops completely collapse on awkward coin sizes. You need DP to build an impregnable table of correct partial states.

bit-manipulation.title: Knowledge Check
bit-manipulation.question: What does x XOR x always equal?
bit-manipulation.successMessage: Spot on. XOR-ing a value cancels itself out, evaporating data directly at the binary level. Pure algorithmic magic.
